sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Ana Life, also called Ana Liffey, is an Irish heroine. She is the River Liffey made into a woman. James Joyce placed her at the centre of his novel Finnegans Wake, where he named her Anna Livia Plurabelle. The invented word “riverrun” opens the book. The ending turns back to the start, like river water flowing to the sea and then returning by rain. Ana Life is not Joyce’s invention. She is the only female face among the river gods carved on Dublin’s bridges. Her name joins two older names: Anu, an early Irish land goddess, and Lífe, the Irish name of the river. The carving is the most mythically accurate of the bridge figures, because Irish rivers are almost always goddesses, not kings. The Liffey goddess is named Lífe. The river rises in the Bog of Allen, not in the Devil’s Glen in Wicklow as Joyce wrote. It flows south, then west, then north, then east, and pours into the sea.
objective: Record Ana Life, the Irish river heroine.
